Mom's Hospital Papers, Dates and Contacts, in One Place

A one-page inventory of what you've been handed and told, and what you still need to ask for.

Download PDF

The medication list is in your bag, the social worker's card is in your coat pocket, and the date somebody mentioned is in a text to your brother.

This page doesn't ask you to understand any of it. It asks where each thing is, how recent it is, and who has it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
The discharge plan or discharge papers, in writing
Her diagnoses and the reason for this stay, as they were given to you
The current medication list, and what changed during the stay
The expected discharge date, and who told you
Any other dates you've been given, and who gave each one
Any letter or notice you've been handed about coverage or billing
Mom's Medicare card and any other insurance cards
The discharge planner or social worker: name and phone number
The doctor, nurses and therapists involved: names and roles
The business office: a name and phone number
Who is making healthcare decisions with Mom or for her, and where any paperwork about that is kept
Family members who can help: names, phone numbers, and the days they're free

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each.

For example Nothing in writing about the discharge plan yet. The date we have came from a nurse in passing. Mark will ask the discharge planner on Thursday.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each paper. If it has no date, write “undated” and ask for a current copy.
  • For anything you were told and not handed, write who said it and on which day.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize a document here. Just say where it is.
  • Bring this page and the papers to the discharge conversation.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any paper, notice or instruction means. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the person or office that gave it to you. Nothing here is medical, legal, financial or tax advice.

Ready for the next step?

Where this comes from

The first row follows the Family Caregiver Alliance's discharge guide, which tells families to ask for all instructions and guidance in writing. The rest come from the Medicaid Planning Roadmap's working list for this step.
